pronunciation.approximation: 'FOO-jin' — the first syllable is long and breezy, with lips almost touching for the 'f'; the final 'jin' is quick with a soft 'j'.

pronunciation.note: Fūjin is Tier 1 because the initial ū is long. The name is a straightforward Sino-Japanese compound: 風 (fū, 'wind') + 神 (jin, 'god/spirit'). He is typically paired with Raijin, the thunder god, in Japanese temple and popular art.

domains.title: God of the Wind
domains.subtitle: Storms, Breath, Destruction, and Renewal
domains.lead:
Fūjin is the wind made wild. In Japanese art he appears as a fierce demon, hair streaming, clad in a leopard-skin loincloth, carrying a vast bag of winds on his shoulders. When he opens it, gales tear through forests, scatter roofs, and flatten fields; when he closes it, the air grows still. He is one of the oldest kami in the Japanese pantheon, a destructive force that is also necessary for pollination, dispersal of seeds, and the cleansing of stale air.

He is the brother or counterpart of Raijin, the thunder god, and the two are often depicted together at temple gates, where their terrifying presence keeps danger away from sacred ground.

cards.name: Bag of Winds
cards.desc: He carries a great sack slung over his shoulders; opening it releases the winds of the world.

cards.name: Demon Guardian
cards.desc: His fierce face and muscular body mark him as one of the powerful oni-like kami who protect temples.

cards.name: Companion of Raijin
cards.desc: He is paired with the thunder god at temple gates and in screen paintings, storm and wind as twin forces.

cards.name: Cosmic Breath
cards.desc: Beyond destruction, wind is the breath that moves pollen, carries clouds, and clears the air for new growth.

mythology.lead: Fūjin's mythology is grounded in the creation narratives of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, in esoteric Buddhist iconography, and in the visual tradition of Japanese screen painting. He is both a primordial force and a temple guardian — and, in national memory, the wind itself that twice saved Japan.

myths.title: The Birth of the Wind Kami
myths.text: The wind kami are older than the name Fūjin. In the Kojiki's birth-of-the-kami sequence, the wind god Shina-tsu-hiko (志那都比古) and his partner Shina-tsu-hime are born as Izanagi and Izanami take stock of the elemental kami of the new-made land; the Nihon Shoki preserves the lovelier etiology — Izanagi, looking out over the country he had made, found it wrapped in morning mist, breathed, and blew the fog away, and that first breath became the wind god. The thunder kami have a harsher nativity: when the fire god Kagutsuchi burned his mother Izanami to death, Izanagi cut him down, and from the sword's blood were born the thunder gods, among them Takemikazuchi — born, like storm's own electricity, from the catastrophe of fire itself. The demonic figure called Fūjin — leopard skin, wind-bag, streaming hair — is the later, Buddhist-inflected portrait of these older kami of the moving air.

myths.title: The Cave and the Returning Winds
myths.text:
When Amaterasu hid herself in the heavenly rock-cave (Ama-no-Iwato), the world did not merely lose its light — it lost its motion: the kami assembled in the dark, and the very winds of heaven stilled with everything else. The ritual comedy by which the goddess was lured back — the cock, the mirror, Ame-no-Uzume's dance on an upturned tub — is therefore also a weather-myth: when the cave door opened, light returned with wind, rain, and the movement of all things (Kojiki; Aston's Nihongi).

The medieval tradition that paired Fūjin with Raijin at temple gates read this old story into architecture: wind and thunder stand together at the threshold because both are signs that the hidden has come back out. A temple gate with Fūjin on one side and Raijin on the other is a frozen Ama-no-Iwato — kept open.

myths.title: Fūten, Guardian of the Directions
myths.text:
In esoteric Buddhism the wind god is Fūten, one of the Twelve Devas (jūniten) who stand guard around the mandala, assigned in the Japanese tradition to the north-west. He is the Vedic Vāyu carried east along the Silk Road — the Indian wind god appears among the outer guardians of the Womb-realm mandala — and Japan re-dressed him in the kami's leopard skin and gave him Raijin for a brother. Temples fixed the pair in the national imagination: Kanō Tan'yū's wind-and-thunder paintings at Sanjūsangen-dō in Kyōto and Tawaraya Sōtatsu's celebrated Fūjin-Raijin folding screens at Kennin-ji turn two directional guardians into an eternal weather-front.

In the mandala, Fūten's work is apotropaic: he sweeps the ground clean of obstacles before the rite begins — the wind as the broom of the sacred.

myths.title: The Winds That Saved Japan
myths.text:
In 1274 and again in 1281, the Mongol fleets of Kublai Khan stood off Japan's shores, and both times great typhoons smashed the invading armadas at anchor. Medieval Japan named the deliverance kamikaze — the divine wind — and temple tradition credited the storm kami with the victory: the very winds that Fūjin keeps in his bag. Court and shrine celebrated the miracles (the Hachiman and Kasuga cults each claimed the credit), and the government's prayers at Iwashimizu and elsewhere had, in effect, been answered by weather. The episode matters for Fūjin because it moved him from the mandala's margin to the center of national memory: the wind-bag god became the patron of a country's survival.

Modern scholarship reads the typhoons soberly as meteorology, but the medieval reading — that Japan's storms were its gods — shaped Japanese identity for seven centuries, down to the word's darkest reuse in 1944.

lore.syncretism: Fūjin descends from the Chinese wind deity Fengshen, transmitted to Japan along with Buddhism and continental iconography. He also resembles wind gods across Eurasia, from the Greek Boreas and the Vedic Vāta to the Central Asian wind demons depicted on Silk Road textiles. In Japan, however, he became thoroughly domesticated as a kami, paired with Raijin and rendered in a distinctive visual style by artists such as Tawaraya Sōtatsu and Ogata Kōrin. The Japanese fascination with storms — wind, rain, thunder, lightning — produced one of the most dynamic bodies of religious painting in East Asia, with Fūjin and Raijin at its center.
lore.culturalLegacy: Fūjin remains one of Japan's most recognizable kami. Tawaraya Sōtatsu's celebrated Wind-and-Thunder folding screen (early 17th century), preserved at Kennin-ji in Kyōto, is a national treasure and an icon of Japanese art; Kanō Tan'yū's depictions at Sanjūsangen-dō are nearly as famous. Temples still display the pair at gates and in festival processions, and Fūjin appears in manga, anime, video games, and advertising as a symbol of overwhelming natural force. The word kamikaze — the 'divine wind' of 1274 and 1281 — is his modern inheritance, both as miracle and as warning. The Unicode restoration Fūjin preserves the long vowel that distinguishes this divine name from the ordinary homographs fujin (婦人 'women'; 夫人 'wife').
lore.extendedMeditation:
Fūjin is the god of the air we cannot see but cannot live without. His bag of winds contains both destruction and renewal: the gale that uproots trees also scatters seeds, the storm that sinks ships also clears the sky. He is a reminder that the atmosphere is not empty space but a living force.

To contemplate Fūjin is to feel the wind as sacred. Every breath, every gust, every seasonal shift becomes a meeting with an ancient power. He does not ask for worship in stillness; he is worshipped in motion, in the visible effects of the invisible. And when a typhoon turns aside from the coast, his oldest lesson returns: the same breath that destroys can also be the one that saves.

lore.archaeology: Fūjin is best known from Japanese painting and sculpture rather than from archaeological contexts alone. The oldest surviving depictions appear in Heian- and Kamakura-period Buddhist iconography, where he serves as a guardian deity. The most famous visual testimony is the pair of folding screens by Tawaraya Sōtatsu (early 17th century), preserved at Kennin-ji temple in Kyōto, which depict Fūjin and Raijin in gold-leaf clouds. Temple sculptures and ema (votive plaques) across Japan preserve popular representations of the wind god, while the textual record in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki anchors his mythological origins in the creation age.
lore.cult: Fūjin's cult is a layered one — kami beneath, Buddhist guardian above. The oldest layer is the wind kami of the Kojiki, Shina-tsu-hiko, long-lived lord of the moving air, who is still enshrined at Tatsuta Taisha in the hills west of Nara, where the autumn gales and falling maples have marked his season for a millennium; the Engi-shiki, the early tenth-century register of official shrines, lists the wind gods among the kami once receiving state offerings. Above that layer rides esoteric Buddhism: as Fūten, one of the Twelve Devas guarding the mandala's circumference, the wind god received temple rites and directional liturgies from the Tendai and Shingon schools, stationed at the north-west of the Womb-realm mandala to sweep obstacles from the ritual ground. No single great pilgrimage cult formed around him — his worship dispersed into the storm-prayers of the coasts, the protective pairing with Raijin at temple gates, and the national thanksgiving of 1274 and 1281, when the typhoons that broke the Mongol fleets were read as the wind god's own answer to prayer.
lore.iconography: Learn the bag and you will know him anywhere: Fūjin shoulders a great sack of winds — the fūtaku — and everything else in his portrait serves the gale. His hair streams back from a demon's face, green or red of skin, a leopard skin knotted at the waist, the whole body twisted as if leaning into his own storm. The formula is Buddhist in its Japanese form: as Fūten of the Twelve Devas he appears in late Heian and Kamakura jūniten sets — the celebrated Twelve Kings of Jingo-ji on Mount Takao in Kyōto preserve the type — standing at his station with the sack. The bag itself is older than Japan: Chinese art had long pictured the wind earl Fengbo shouldering a wind-sack, and the motif travelled east with continental Buddhism. Medieval temple architecture made him a gate-guardian, always paired with Raijin, thunder against wind. The great screens of the seventeenth century then gave the pair the whole sky — gold-leaf clouds at Kennin-ji in Sōtatsu's hand, the long wall of Sanjūsangen-dō in Kanō Tan'yū's — one gale, one thunder-roll, frozen at full force.
lore.reception: Fūjin is a traveller who was naturalized. His road begins in India with Vāyu, the Vedic wind, rides the Silk Road through China's wind god Fengbo — the sack-shouldered earl already old in Han art — and arrives with Buddhism in sixth-century Japan, where esoteric doctrine stationed him as Fūten among the Twelve Devas of the mandala. The eighth century naturalized him: the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki re-founded the wind as Shina-tsu-hiko, born in the divine age of Izanagi's first breath, so that Buddhist guardian and native kami came to share one body and one bag of winds. Heian liturgy, Kamakura gate architecture, and the storm-prayers of the coasts carried him through the Middle Ages until 1274 and 1281 made him a national patron, the typhoons read as the gods' own defense of the islands. The early modern age raised him from guardian to masterpiece: the Rinpa painters of the seventeenth century fixed the Fūjin–Raijin screen as a summit of Japanese art, and modern scholarship — Chamberlain's Kojiki (1882), Aston's Nihongi (1896), Philippi's translation a century on — has given the wind god an unbroken critical tradition from the chronicles to the present.
